This is the most widely distributed species of Sarcochilus and also the most common. Being such a widely distributed species, this orchid exhibits significant variation in flowering time, plant habit, floral morphology and fragrance (see also S. niveus). Variable morphological features include flower size, tepal size and shape, labellum size, shape of the lateral lobes, blunt or pointed apex on the labellum midlobe, and patterns of colour on the labellum. Walsh (1998) draws attention to a variant with light to heavy purple striations and other marks on the labellum apex (sometimes solid purple), strong mustard yellow colouration on the lateral lobes and an intense vanilla-like fragrance. He records this variant as occurring between Dorrigo Plateau and Barrington Tops at around 600 m altitude, but it also occurs as far south as Robertson in the southern tablelands at around 730 m. Some plants with a pinkish blush to the flowers have been found at Dorrigo, N.S.W. and Kroombit Tops, Qld. Floral perfumes vary from a strong, sweet, spicy fragrance to resembling that of orange-blossom or vanilla essence or simply unpleasant. Aerial growths can develop on aborted racemes. For an inspired treatise and lovely photos of Sarcochilus falcatus see Walsh (1998).

Fitzgerald (1888) studied the pollination of Spiranthes australis in the vicinity of Sydney, the type location for the species, and concluded that the pollinia were so tightly encased in the anther that they could not be extracted and the flowers were self-pollinating - in his very unusual and descriptive wording ‘in my opinion it is never made fruitful by the pollen from another flower.’ However, the self-pollination process in these central N.S.W. plants is not straightforward because there is no obvious rostellum separating the anther and the stigma and the pollen grains do not simply fall onto the stigma or come into contact with its upper surface. It is quite possible these plants are apomictic. By contrast, plants from some areas have functional pollinia attached to a removable viscidium and are probably insect-pollinated; in others the viscidium is abortive meaning that the pollinarium cannot be extracted from the flowers as a unit. Flowers of this latter type can also have loosely packed, friable pollinia and are commonly either self-pollinating via the pollen falling onto the stigma, or apomictic. Insect-pollinated flowers of S. australis are often visited by small, dark, native bees which work their way upward on the spikes, probing deep into the flowers for nectar and during the process picking up pollinia on the face around the mouthparts. Michael (1964), after studying many of the populations across southern Australia, concluded that ''considerable'' variation existed within Australia, with differences in markings on the sepals, size and colouring of the petals, and differences in shape and markings on the leaflets. Peirce (1973, cited in Pierce 1997) identified additional variation in the leaflets illustrated by Michael (1964), from 6 to 13, in Western Australia. According to Michael (1964), the Australian populations are comprised predominantly of the short-styled pentaploid morph, and that as far as is known the pentaploid variant exists in only the short-styled morph. Michael (1964) also found that a mid-styled morph is also present in Australia. A number of flora accounts (e.g. Bennett 1987, Conn 1992, Conn et al. 1997) note that fruit was either not seen or not known in Australia. However, Michael (1964) found that in situations where different style-length forms are present, seed is freely produced. Jaspars (1986) notes that: "2 chromosome races occur here. The largest populations are the short-styled sterile pentaploids (5n = 35); there are also small populations of fertile tetraploids (4n = 28) with all 3 style-lengths."

Bird dispersed seeds. Extract from an article by Sara Freeland highlighting the importance of this plant to the Green Parrot's ecosystem on Norfolk Island: "An intriguing behaviour has been observed in Norfolk Island's Green Parrots (Cyanoramphus cookii). Birds have been spotted using native pepper trees (Piper excelsum) to help fend off pests and parasites. Green parrots were photographed and filmed biting off pieces of pepper tree shoots and bark, chewing them, and then rubbing the chewed material through their feathers. They also stripped leaves and rubbed their beaks along the branches before applying preen oil over themselves. Pepper Trees are known for their potent aromatic compounds, particularly piperine, which has insect-repellent and antimicrobial properties. This behaviour of self-anointing with plant material appears to help the parrots repel blood-sucking insects and other ectoparasites. While birds are known to use various methods to combat parasites, such as preening, dust-bathing, and anting (where they use ants to help clean their feathers), the use of plant materials for anointing is quite rare. Historical records and recent observations show that this behaviour is not entirely new but has been noted infrequently across different bird species - including some parrots in New Zealand and Darwin’s finches."

This species is superficially very similar to Bursaria spinosa subsp. lasiophylla and sterile, juvenile and intermediate herbarium specimens of that taxon are virtually indistinguishable. Important understory shrubs in eucalypt woodlands throughout Australia. Recorded as being eaten by cattle, but early botanists noted that the spinescent short shoots tend to persist to just past the height of browsing animals. Juvenile and intermediate forms can be involved in complex ant-butterfly interactions, e.g. as host of the pupae of the endangered dull copper butterfly, Paralucia pyrodiscus and the even rarer Eltham copper, Paralucia pyrodiscus lucida.

Bursaria spinosa is one of the few wide ranging species in this family, and is widespread and common in the understory of open Eucalypt woodlands, in all but alpine or more arid inland regions. Two subspecies are recognised: the autonym (Bursaria spinosa subsp. spinosa) occurs on a variety of soil types, generally excluding heavier clay soils at higher altitudes in tablelands and lower mountain ranges in south-eastern Australia, where it is replaced by Bursaria spinosa subsp. lasiophylla.

Subsp, lasiophylla may represent a clinal form of the common glabrous subspecies. Pittosporum undulatum has a vigorous rhizomatous root system which survives all but the most intense wild fires, and a habit of holding the large leaves of its coppice growth horizontal blocks light for other seeds to germinate. This ensures very rapid colonisation, particularly on disturbed sites (Gleadow 1982). For details on biology and ecology see Mullett (2009) and references therein.

In 1956, R.C. Cooper stated that Pittosporum undulatum was naturally occurring in marginal rainforest throughout the coastal ranges of southeastern Australia. Grows in wet sclerophyll to sheltered dry sclerophyll forests and scrubs.

Originally southeastern Australia, from McPherson range in Southern Queensland to Victorian Alps in south-eastern Victoria. Declared a weed in Victoria. Restricting horticultural plantings to just male plants is not a solution as most of these plants also produce occasional fruits; all forms are self-compatible and plants range from dioecious to monoecious. Neither the recent morphological nor the DNA analyses are informative on the affinities of this species. Noticeably the two truly wide-ranging/weedy Pittosporum species in Australia (P. undulatum and P. ferrugineum) both display the full spectrum of sex strategies from unisexual flowers with staminode or pistillode tissue, to perfect and clearly viable bisexual flowers, often in the same inflorescence. Hybrids are becoming more frequent between Pittosporum bicolor and P. undulatum as the latter continues its range expansion. Pittosporum bicolor has rather narrow elliptic leaves with a persistent indumentum on the undersurface, maroon streaked yellow flowers and black fruits with red seeds. Hybrids between these two taxa tend to have bicolor foliage (although wider and often longer), undulatum flowers (complete with vestigial staminodes) and fruits with orange seeds. For an account of Pittosporum undulatum on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands, where introduced and escaped from cultivation, see Green (1994: 158).

Alopecurus aequalis is spread mainly by seed. Overseas it is a weed of crops, particularly in rice fields where it is a floating weed seed species (the seeds being dispersed by irrigation waters) (Li & Qiang 2009), and cereals such as wheat, barley and oats (Holm et al. 1997). It is a serious winter annual weed in both lowland and upland crops in Japan, and a major rice weed in Nepal (to 1900 m altitude) and the Philippines, as well as infesting rice in China, Taiwan and Hungary, and vegetables and vineyards (Holm et al. 1997). As a competitive weed A. aequalis can reduce cereal yields. The presence of this grass in the Murrumbidgee-Murray irrigation area and Riverina could indicate a potential for further spread and weed issues. Alopecurus aequalis is also an environmental weed, having been recorded in damp or ponded areas in eucalypt woodlands and on saltbush plains in New South Wales (based on herbarium records) and mallee bioregions in Victoria (The State of Victoria Department of Sustainability and Environment 2009), as well as creeks in a boggy subalpine area in Kosciuszko National Park. It is able to grow in shallow aquatic habitats.

Grows in wet places, including swampy areas, bogs, shallow pools, poorly drained areas (e.g. ponded or depressed areas on plains in native woodlands and shrublands), along streams, creeks and irrigation channels; to high altitudes; often aquatic with partly submerged stems.

Introduced; occurs in southeastern South Australia, western to northeastern Victoria and in the Kosciuszko area possibly W to far southwestern New South Wales. Native to most of Europe, Asia and N America; also naturalised in New Zealand.

The presence and distribution of Alopecurus aequalis in New South Wales and possibly elsewhere in Australia requires further investigation. There are specimens from the Cooleman Plain in Kosciuszko National Park with awns to 2 mm long attached just below the middle of the lemma at c. ⅖ of the lemma length from the base (similar to what occurs in A. aequalis specimens from overseas examined by P.G.K.). There is another group of specimens, often previously determined as A. geniculatus, which also have inconspicuous lemma awns and these specimens are from the Yanco-Berrigan-Hay-Barham area of the South Western Plains and probably extend west to Wentworth in the South Far Western Plains, e.g. 7.7 km SE along Conargo-Deniliquin (Jerilderie) road from the Cobb Hwy, M.F. Porteners 9009011 & V. Logan (NSW). In these specimens the straight to slightly recurved or outswept awns are often shorter (to 1.5 (-2) mm long), attached in the upper half of the lemma near the apex (to c. 0.5 (-0.7) mm below the apex) and usually more conspicuously exceed the apex of the glumes (i.e. extend further), and the folded glumes are characteristically slightly sigmoid in shape (the different spikelet forms are illustrated in Kodela 2015: 145, fig. 2). This latter group of specimens possibly represent another taxon, but the specimens have not been able to be matched with any other species of Alopecurus from exotic specimens held at MEL and NSW or from following the revision of the genus by Doğan (1999). Alternatively, they may simply reflect variation in A. aequalis where the lemma awn can be inserted from c. midway to subapical. This variation also occurs in Victoria, where specimens with awns inserted higher on the lemma (as in most of the southwestern New South Wales specimens) mainly come from the northwest of the State, fide N.G. Walsh (pers. comm.); see also Kodela (2015) for further discussion. There is also the possibility for hybrids between A. aequalis and A. geniculatus (= A. ×haussknechtianus Asch. & Graebn.). Alopecurus aequalis possibly also occurs in Tasmania as several specimens labelled as A. geniculatus have barely exserted, straight awns, e.g. Brumbys Creek, R.C. Gunn 1459 (NSW); Queenstown, c. 1932, D. Martin (NSW). The biostatus of Alopecurus aequalis in Australia (where collection records go back to c. 1880) warrants further investigation (see Kodela 2015 and notes under genus). Alopecurus aequalis is non toxic.

Amphipogon caricinus is closely related to A. strictus, from which it differs primarily in having intravaginal shoots often developing successively to produce obliquely ascending rhizomes, and often also further shoots from sheaths above the basal one. Additional features include generally longer panicles and a lack of large setae on glumes. Vickery (1950) also used as a differentiating feature the cilia on lobes of the lemma and palea continuing to the tip in A. caricinus var. caricinus, but tending to end before the apex, leaving a short scabrous tip in A. strictus. I have found this feature to be unreliable. In the zone where the ranges of the two species approach each other or overlap (e.g. south-eastern S.A. and the W.A. wheatbelt E and ESE of Perth), identification can be difficult, with plants bearing A. caricinus rhizomes sometimes having setae on the glumes. Despite these occasional unresolved difficulties, the two species are considered distinct. They can sometimes be found growing together and are readily distinguishable in their overlap zones. A variant in the Geraldton-Northampton area of W.A. has the rhizome structure of this species although the rhizome and lower sheaths are exceptionally hairy, and the glumes resemble those of A. strictus. This variant, placed in A. caricinus var. caricinus in this treatment, requires further study. Thereare two varieties.

Previously described as an annual, D. aegyptium frequently assumes a perennial, stoloniferous habit in Australia, and has been confused with the perennial D. australe. Dried specimens of E. ramosus are most reliably distinguished from those of E. acicularis by the combination of completely glabrous foliage (except for occasional hairs behind the ligule) and the absence of an external ligule. In addition, E. ramosus tends to be taller, with fewer spikes, and the culms branching at several nodes is distinctive in more mature specimens. The two species may be more readily distinguished in the field, as the spikes of E. ramosus are reported to spread in a single plane while those of E. acicularis are arranged in several planes. Like some other Australian species of Eragrostis, the panicle of E. elongata has two forms: spiciform, with the spikelets in dense, often globular clusters along the axis, and open, with the spikelets somewhat crowded along widely spreading or appressed primary branches. The former is more common, but the latter is seen in the type specimen. Distinguishing features include the form of the panicles; granular lemma and palea; heavy-textured glumes with thickened, scabrous keel; usually two stamens; and spikelets with a median depression above the rachilla. It intergrades with both the E. brownii/E. benthamii complex and with E. sororia. Eragrostis elongata and E. sororia can both be distinguished from the former complex in their typical condition by the presence of only two stamens, the shape and size of their grains, and their compactly spiciform panicles. Unlike E. elongata, in typical E. sororia the spikelets are inflated and gibbous, the paleas are orbicular, pouched and smooth, and the lemmas and anthers are larger.
